name: Iterator
intent: Visit the elements of a collection one by one without exposing how the collection is stored.
scenario: A playlist can be played forward or in reverse, and two listeners can walk the same playlist independently.
problem: The client loops over the playlist's internal array with indexes. That ties the loop to the array: if the playlist becomes a linked list or a database cursor, every loop breaks. Reverse order and two simultaneous walkers need extra index bookkeeping in the client.
solution: Give the playlist methods that return an Iterator with hasNext() and next(). Each iterator remembers its own position. The client asks for an iterator and loops until hasNext() is false, never touching the storage. Different iterators give different orders.
pain: The client loops over internal array indexes
Changing the collection's storage breaks every loop
Reverse order means rewriting the loop with different index math
Two walkers need two separate index variables managed by the caller
benefits: The client only uses hasNext() and next()
Storage can change freely behind the playlist
Reverse, filtered or shuffled traversals are just other iterators
Each iterator keeps its own position, so walkers are independent
whenToUse: You want to hide a collection's internal structure from clients
You need several traversal orders or simultaneous traversals
You want one uniform way to walk different kinds of collections
whenNotToUse: A plain array and a for-of loop are enough
The language already provides what you need (it usually does)
You only ever need one fixed traversal
pitfalls: Changing the collection while iterating can skip or repeat elements
Overkill in languages with built-in iteration support
Hand-written iterators are more code than a generator or yield return
External iterators need the caller to remember to check hasNext()

roles.label: Concrete Iterator
roles.description: Implements one traversal and remembers its position.

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Walks the collection through the Iterator interface.

quiz.question: A playlist screen loops with an index over the playlist's internal array. The team moves the tracks into a paged database result, and every loop in the app breaks. What change prevents this from happening again?
options: Have the playlist return an iterator, and loop with hasNext and next so storage stays private
Keep the index loops but add a getTrack(i) method that fetches page after page by position
Return the playlist's database cursor to callers so that they can step through the rows
Copy all tracks into a fresh array on every call so the loops keep working as they did
quiz.explanation: An iterator hides how the tracks are stored, so the next storage change touches only the playlist. getTrack(i) keeps clients tied to positions, and it may be slow with paged storage. Exposing the cursor ties every loop to the database.

quiz.question: Two listeners walk the same 100-track playlist at once. One plays in order and the other in shuffled order, and each must continue from where it stopped. Where should each walker's current position be kept?
options: In its own iterator object, so each walk has independent state over the same playlist
In the playlist as a currentIndex field, protected with a lock so that two listeners can share it
In the playlist as a map from listener name to position, updated when the listener is called
In a copy of the playlist for each listener, so that each copy can keep its own index
quiz.explanation: Each iterator remembers its position, so several traversals of different orders can run over one collection. Storing positions in the playlist makes the collection do bookkeeping for its clients. Copying the playlist wastes memory and gets stale.

quiz.question: A single-threaded job removes expired items from a list by calling list.remove inside a loop driven by an iterator. Some expired items are left behind, and no error is raised. What is the cause and the best fix?
options: The iterator counts items twice, so the fix is to call reset on it after every removal
hasNext returns the wrong value after a removal, so the fix is to check the list size instead
Removal shifts items past the position, so remove through the iterator
The iterator is not thread safe, so the fix is to wrap each call to next in a lock
quiz.explanation: Changing the collection behind an iterator's back moves elements under its position, so some are skipped. The iterator's own remove, or a pass that collects then removes, keeps positions consistent. There is only one thread, so a lock changes nothing.
